subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 68-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because of new confusion. On examination she is alert but disoriented. She cannot state the current date or year. When asked where she is, she incorrectly says she is at home, though she is in the hospital. She correctly identifies herself and recognizes her daughter. Her serum sodium is 122 mEq/L.
question: Which of the following best describes the typical order in which the components of orientation are lost in this patient?

options.text: Person first, then place, then time
Place first, then person, then time
Time first, then place, then person
Time first, then person, then place
All three components are lost simultaneously and in no particular order

explanation_correct: Orientation is the ability to know the date and time, where one is, and who one is. The components are lost in a predictable order: time first, then place, and finally person. In this patient the date is already incorrect (time lost) and the location is wrong (place lost), while self-identification is still intact (person preserved). This pattern is consistent with a metabolic cause such as the hyponatremia described. Loss of orientation may result from alcohol, drugs, fluid/electrolyte imbalance, head trauma, hypoglycemia, infection, nutritional deficiencies, or hypoxia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Person is generally the last aspect of orientation to be lost, not the first.
explanation_incorrect.B: Time is lost before place, and person is typically the last component to be lost.
explanation_incorrect.D: Place is lost before person; the typical sequence is time, then place, then person.
explanation_incorrect.E: Orientation is lost in a characteristic sequence rather than randomly or all at once.

educationalObjective: Recall that orientation is lost in the order time, then place, then person.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 45-year-old man is evaluated after a motorcycle accident in which he struck his head. He is now alert and can carry on a normal conversation and learn new information, but he has no memory of the events that occurred in the 30 minutes before the collision. His memory of his childhood and of earlier adult life is intact.
question: Which of the following best describes this patient's memory deficit?

options.text: Anterograde amnesia — inability to form new memories after the insult
Retrograde amnesia — inability to recall events that occurred before the insult
Dissociative amnesia — psychogenic loss of personal information
Korsakoff syndrome — confabulation due to thiamine deficiency
Simple inattention secondary to delirium

explanation_correct: Retrograde amnesia is the inability to remember things that occurred before a CNS insult. This patient cannot recall the minutes preceding his head injury yet can acquire new memories and retains remote memories, which is the classic pattern of retrograde amnesia. By contrast, anterograde amnesia is an inability to remember things occurring after an insult, with reduced acquisition of new memory. Korsakoff syndrome is a chronic amnestic state due to thiamine deficiency with confabulation, and dissociative amnesia is a psychogenic loss of personal information following severe stress.

explanation_incorrect.A: Anterograde amnesia impairs formation of new memories after the insult; this patient forms new memories normally.
explanation_incorrect.C: Dissociative amnesia is a psychogenic inability to recall important personal information after severe trauma, not after a documented head injury.
explanation_incorrect.D: Korsakoff syndrome is due to thiamine (B1) deficiency with confabulation in chronic alcohol use, not acute trauma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Delirium involves fluctuating attention and arousal, both of which are intact in this patient.

educationalObjective: Differentiate retrograde amnesia (loss of memories before an insult) from anterograde amnesia (loss of new memory formation after an insult).

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 62-year-old man with a long history of alcohol use disorder presents with confusion and disorientation. He is unable to learn new information, and his recall of events from before the onset of his illness is comparatively preserved. When questioned about his hospitalization, he confidently invents elaborate stories that did not happen.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's condition?

options.text: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency with destruction of the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus
Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency with degeneration of the hippocampus and amygdala
Vitamin B12 deficiency with demyelination of the dorsal columns
Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency limited to the cerebral cortex with sparing of limbic structures
Folate deficiency with disruption of the anterior thalamus and mammillary bodies

explanation_correct: This patient has Korsakoff syndrome, a late neuropsychiatric manifestation of Wernicke encephalopathy seen in chronic alcohol use. It is caused by vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency and produces amnesia with anterograde impairment greater than retrograde impairment, along with disorientation. There is disruption and destruction of limbic system structures, especially the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus. Confabulation, the fabrication of detailed false accounts without intent to deceive, is characteristic.

explanation_incorrect.B: Korsakoff syndrome is due to thiamine (B1), not niacin (B3) deficiency; niacin deficiency causes pellagra.
explanation_incorrect.C: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration with dorsal column demyelination, not an amnestic confabulating syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thiamine deficiency in Korsakoff syndrome disrupts limbic structures (mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus) rather than being limited to cortex with limbic sparing.
explanation_incorrect.E: Folate deficiency is not the cause of Korsakoff syndrome; the responsible vitamin is thiamine (B1).

educationalObjective: Recognize Korsakoff syndrome as thiamine deficiency causing anterograde-predominant amnesia, disorientation, and confabulation with mammillary body and anterior thalamic damage in chronic alcoholism.

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 70-year-old woman is admitted with acute confusion and disorientation. Her daughter reports the patient has had poor oral intake and has recently started a medication with strong anticholinergic effects. Laboratory studies reveal a serum glucose of 38 mg/dL. The resident notes that disorientation has many potential causes.
question: Which of the following is NOT a commonly cited cause of loss of orientation?

options.text: Hypoglycemia
Fluid and electrolyte imbalance
Hypoxia
Nutritional deficiency
Essential hypertension

explanation_correct: Common causes of loss of orientation include alcohol, drugs, fluid/electrolyte imbalance, head trauma, hypoglycemia, infection, nutritional deficiencies, and hypoxia. Essential hypertension, particularly when chronic, is not a typical direct cause of acute disorientation. In this patient the hypoglycemia, probable nutritional deficiency from poor intake, and anticholinergic medication are all plausible contributors to her disorientation.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hypoglycemia is a well-recognized cause of disorientation and altered mental status.
explanation_incorrect.B: Fluid and electrolyte disturbances such as hyponatremia commonly cause disorientation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypoxia can produce confusion and disorientation as cortical function is compromised.
explanation_incorrect.D: Nutritional deficiencies such as thiamine deficiency can cause disorientation, as in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

educationalObjective: Recall the common causes of disorientation and recognize that essential hypertension is not among them.
